title: Money: From Barter to Modern Currency

questions.question: The 'double coincidence of wants' is a problem associated with:
questions.rationale: Barter requires each trader to want exactly what the other offers at the same time and place — money removes this constraint.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary function of money?
questions.rationale: The primary functions are medium of exchange and unit of value; deferred payment, transfer, and storing value are secondary.

questions.question: Modern currency notes are an example of:
options: Representative money backed fully by gold
questions.rationale: Fiat money derives value from government legal-tender order, not from the material or a gold backing.

questions.question: Cheques and bank deposits that are accepted on trust in the issuer are called:
questions.rationale: Fiduciary money circulates on confidence in the issuer rather than legal-tender law — cheques are the classic case.

questions.question: In India, narrow money M1 consists of:
options: Currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI
questions.rationale: M1 = currency with the public plus demand deposits with banks plus other deposits with the RBI — the most spendable money.

questions.question: Which measure is called broad money in India?
questions.rationale: M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks; it is the headline measure of money supply.

questions.question: High-powered money (monetary base) consists of:
options: Currency with public plus cash reserves with banks and the RBI
questions.rationale: M0 is currency with the public plus banks' cash reserves held with themselves and with the RBI — the base banks multiply.

questions.question: The RBI has followed the minimum reserve system of currency issue since:
questions.rationale: Since 1956 the RBI maintains a minimum reserve of ₹200 crore (₹115 crore in gold) and may issue currency against it without limit.

questions.question: Which is NOT a characteristic of good money?
questions.rationale: Good money must be scarce — a money printable without limit would lose value; the other traits are all desirable.

questions.question: A shopkeeper accepts a ₹500 note although the paper and printing cost far less. This works because money is:
options: Commodity money whose paper is valuable
Fiat money backed by RBI and legal-tender status with public confidence
questions.rationale: Fiat money functions on government order plus confidence that others will keep accepting it — the lesson's example of the ₹500 note.
